# How bacteria copy themselves and change

> *Bacteria change in two ways: by errors in copying their own DNA, and by taking in DNA from other
> bacteria. Both happen at random. Drug use then selects whichever cells happen to survive. That
> sequence explains antimicrobial resistance, and also how a harmless strain can acquire a toxin.*

## Copying the genome {#sec-gen-copy}

A typical bacterium carries one circular chromosome. That of *Escherichia coli* has about
4.6 million base pairs and some 4,300 genes. Many bacteria also carry **plasmids**: small, circular
DNA molecules that replicate on their own and often carry genes the cell can live without, such as
genes for resistance or toxins. Before dividing by binary fission, the cell copies its chromosome,
starting from a single origin and working round the circle in both directions.

From cell biology you know how your own cells turn genes into proteins. Bacteria follow the same
central dogma, with differences that matter clinically.

| Step | Your cells | Bacteria | Why the difference matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where it happens | Transcription in the nucleus, translation in the cytoplasm | Both in the cytoplasm, at the same time: ribosomes start on an mRNA while it is still being made | Gene expression can change within minutes |
| Gene organisation | One gene per mRNA; genes interrupted by introns | Related genes often share one mRNA, as an **operon**; introns are rare | A whole pathway can be switched on at once |
| RNA polymerase | Several polymerases | One core enzyme of a different structure | A target that human cells do not share |
| Ribosomes | 80S (40S and 60S subunits) | 70S (30S and 50S subunits) | A major drug target; mitochondria have bacterial-type ribosomes, which explains some drug side effects |
| DNA supercoiling | Human topoisomerases | DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV | A target with no exact human equivalent |

The right-hand column answers the sixth question for the machinery of inheritance: what does a
bacterium have that your cells lack? The pharmacology block names the drugs that use each target.

## Change by mutation {#sec-gen-mutation}

A **mutation** is a change in the DNA sequence. Most arise as copying errors during replication:
a **point mutation** swaps one base for another, while insertions and deletions add or remove bases.
DNA-based microbes make roughly one new mutation for every 300 genomes copied [@drake1991constant].
That sounds rare, but bacterial populations are huge, and resistance to a single drug can often
arise from any one of several different mutations. In an infection containing billions of bacteria,
resistant mutants are usually present before treatment begins.

Most mutations are neutral or harmful. A few, by chance, alter the protein a drug acts on, so that
the drug binds poorly. Whether the drug is present has no bearing on which mutations occur. Salvador
Luria and Max Delbrück showed this in 1943: the number of resistant bacteria varied wildly between
parallel cultures, in the pattern expected if mutants arise at random during growth and not in
response to the selecting agent [@luria1943mutations]. Joshua and Esther Lederberg later showed it
directly: using replica plating, they picked colonies from a plate that had never been exposed to the
selecting agent and found that they were already resistant [@lederberg1952replica].

Try it below. Grow the population, decide whether resistant cells exist yet, then add the drug.

<div data-island="selection-sim" data-src="/diagrams/selection-sim.yml"></div>

The drug did not make any bacterium resistant. It killed the susceptible cells, and the resistant
ones that were already there grew into the space. This is **selection**. Repeated over many patients
and many courses of treatment, it is how resistance becomes common.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "bacteria mutate in order to survive the drug"
In one study, 81% of undergraduates agreed that bacteria develop mutations *in order to* become
resistant [@richard2017intuitive]. Bacteria have no way of producing the mutation they need. Mutations
arise at random, and the drug selects the cells that happen to carry a useful one. (Stress from some
drugs can raise the overall mutation rate a little, but the mutations are still random with respect to
resistance.) The related belief that the *body* becomes resistant is held by 62.5% of Singapore
residents [@lim2021singaporekap]. Resistance is a property of the bacteria, and resistant bacteria
spread between people.
:::

## Change by gene transfer {#sec-gen-hgt}

Bacteria can also gain whole genes from other bacteria, a process called **horizontal gene transfer**
to distinguish it from vertical inheritance from parent to daughter cell. There are three classic
routes.

**Transformation** is the uptake of free DNA released by dead cells. Some species, including
*Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Neisseria*, are naturally **competent**: they actively take up DNA from
their surroundings. This was the first route discovered, in the experiment at the end of this chapter.

**Transduction** happens when a **bacteriophage** (a virus that infects bacteria) accidentally packages a
piece of its host's DNA and injects it into the next bacterium it infects.

**Conjugation** is the transfer of a plasmid from one cell to another through direct contact, usually
through a thin tube called a pilus. The older name "sex pilus" is misleading: bacteria have no sexes,
and conjugation produces no offspring. It copies a plasmid into a neighbour, which can belong to a
different species.

A fourth process moves genes around inside and between DNA molecules. **Transposons** ("jumping
genes") are DNA segments that can cut or copy themselves into a new position, for example from the
chromosome onto a plasmid, which can then carry them to another cell. Over time, plasmids and
transposons collect several resistance genes together, so one transfer can bring resistance to several
drugs at once.

Gene transfer also moves virulence genes. Clusters of virulence genes that arrived together in this way
are called **pathogenicity islands**. Much of the difference between a harmless gut *E. coli* and a
strain that causes bloody diarrhoea lies in genes of this kind.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-vertical-horizontal.yml"></div>

## Bacteriophages: lytic and lysogenic {#sec-gen-phage}

Bacteriophages, or phages, are the most numerous biological entities on Earth. A phage can follow one
of two paths after injecting its genome:

- In the **lytic cycle**, the phage takes over the cell, makes hundreds of new phages and bursts
  (**lyses**) the cell to release them.
- In the **lysogenic cycle**, the phage genome joins the bacterial chromosome as a **prophage** and is
  copied along with it each time the cell divides. Damage to the bacterium's DNA can later switch the
  prophage to the lytic cycle.

A prophage can change what its host does, which is called **lysogenic conversion**. Several of the
best-known bacterial toxins are encoded by phage genes, not by the bacterium's own chromosome.

| Toxin | Organism | Consequence of lysogenic conversion |
|---|---|---|
| Diphtheria toxin | *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* | Only strains carrying the phage are **toxigenic** (toxin-producing) and cause diphtheria |
| Cholera toxin | *Vibrio cholerae* | The toxin genes arrived on a phage [@waldor1996cholera] |
| Shiga toxins | Some *E. coli*, such as O157:H7 | Phage-borne toxin genes turned a gut commensal into a cause of bloody diarrhoea |
| Pyrogenic exotoxins | *Streptococcus pyogenes* | Phage-borne superantigen genes, behind scarlet fever |

The same species can therefore be harmless or dangerous depending on which phages it carries. This is
the genetic side of the fifth question, *how does damage happen?*

## Resistance: what it is and how it spreads {#sec-gen-resistance}

**Antimicrobial resistance** is the ability of a microbe to grow in the presence of a drug that would
normally inhibit or kill it. Some resistance is **intrinsic**, a property of the whole species: drugs
that act on the cell wall cannot touch *Mycoplasma*, which has none. Most clinically important
resistance is **acquired** by mutation or gene transfer. Whatever its origin, it works in one of four
ways:

| Mechanism | How it works | Usual genetic origin |
|---|---|---|
| Destroy or modify the drug | An enzyme breaks the drug down or blocks its active site | Genes on plasmids and transposons |
| Change the target | The drug's target protein is altered so the drug binds poorly | Mutation, or an acquired gene for a different version of the target (as in MRSA) |
| Keep the drug out | Fewer **porins** (channels in the Gram-negative outer membrane) let less drug in | Mutation |
| Pump the drug out | **Efflux pumps** in the membrane expel the drug | Mutation increasing pump production, or acquired pump genes |

Three features of resistance follow from this chapter. Every use of an antimicrobial, in people or in
animals, selects resistant bacteria. Resistance genes on plasmids spread between species, so selection
in one organism can create resistance in another. And resistance often carries a cost: without the drug,
resistant bacteria may grow a little more slowly, which is one reason reducing drug use can help, although
many resistance genes persist for years.

**Antimicrobial stewardship** is the coordinated effort to use antimicrobials only when they are
needed, in the right dose and for the right duration, so that selection is kept to a minimum. Because it
works at the level of populations, it depends on every prescriber, not on infection specialists alone.
The pharmacology block covers the drugs and the details.
